category.name: Physical & social engineering
category.description: On-site intrusions and human manipulation: tailgating, rogue devices, badge misuse, vishing, help desk pretexting and USB drops.

playbooks.name: Unauthorized person tailgated into a secured office area
playbooks.summary: Use when someone followed an employee through a badge-controlled door without badging, was seen inside, and you need to know where they went and what they touched.

preparation: Keep CCTV footage for at least 30 days on doors to secure areas
Send badge reader events to the SIEM with door names and badge holder IDs
Agree with facilities on who can pull CCTV and badge logs at short notice
identification: Pull CCTV for the entry door at the reported time and capture images of the person
Match the entry against badge logs to identify which employee badged in with them
Trace the person's route through internal cameras and note rooms entered
Interview the employee who held the door and any staff who spoke with the person
Check the visitor log and reception sign-in for a matching name
containment: Have security escort the person out if still on site and record their details
Sweep the rooms they entered for left-behind devices, cables or USB drives
Check desks and printers in those rooms for missing documents or equipment
eradication: Inspect network ports and conference room equipment in visited areas for rogue devices
Lock workstations left unlocked in the visited area and check them for new logins
Report the intrusion to police if theft or damage is found
recovery: Confirm all equipment in visited areas is accounted for
Reissue access instructions to staff on challenging people without visible badges
Restore normal door operation after any temporary guard posting
lessons: Record which door was tailgated and whether it has anti-tailgating hardware
Add a door-held-open alarm alert to the SOC queue for that entrance
Run a follow-up tailgating test to measure staff challenge rates

splunk.title: Badge events at the door around the intrusion time
splunk.spl: index=physical sourcetype=<badge_system> door="<door_name>" earliest=<start_time> latest=<end_time> | table _time badge_id cardholder event_type door

splunk.title: Door held or forced open alarms
splunk.spl: index=physical sourcetype=<badge_system> event_type IN (door_held_open, door_forced_open) earliest=-30d | stats count by door event_type | sort - count

splunk.title: Network port activity in visited rooms
splunk.spl: index=network sourcetype=cisco:ios ("%LINK-3-UPDOWN" OR "%DOT1X") host=<access_switch> earliest=<start_time> | table _time host interface message

playbooks.name: Rogue device found plugged into the network
playbooks.summary: Use when staff find an unfamiliar small computer, wireless access point, or network implant connected to a port, power strip or behind equipment, possibly left by an intruder.

preparation: Enable 802.1X or NAC on wired ports so unknown devices land in a quarantine VLAN
Keep switch port mapping current so a MAC address can be traced to a wall jack
Set up wireless intrusion detection for rogue access points
identification: Photograph the device in place, including cables, labels and the port it uses
Record the device MAC address and look it up in DHCP leases and switch MAC tables
Find the first time the MAC appeared on the network and what IPs it used
Review firewall logs for outbound connections from the device, such as VPN or cellular backhaul
Pull CCTV and badge logs for the area to find who placed the device
containment: Shut down the switch port the device is connected to
Block the device's outbound destinations at the firewall
Bag the device as evidence with chain of custody without powering it on again
eradication: Hunt for traffic from the device's IP to internal servers and treat accessed systems as exposed
Reset credentials for any service the device captured traffic from
Sweep other network closets and conference rooms for similar devices
recovery: Re-enable the port with NAC enforcement
Hand the device to forensics or law enforcement for analysis
Confirm no further unknown MAC addresses on the access layer
lessons: Record why the port allowed an unknown device and fix NAC coverage gaps
Add a detection for new MAC addresses on access switches outside change windows
Review physical access to the area where the device was found

splunk.title: DHCP leases for the rogue MAC
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=DhcpSrvLog OR sourcetype=infoblox:dhcp dest_mac="<mac_address>" | stats min(_time) as first max(_time) as last values(dest_ip) as ips values(dest_nt_host) as names | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

splunk.title: Outbound traffic from the device
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.src_ip=<device_ip> by All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | sort - bytes_out

splunk.title: Internal systems contacted by the device
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=pan:traffic src_ip=<device_ip> dest_zone=internal | stats count values(dest_port) as ports by dest_ip app

playbooks.name: Help desk socially engineered into resetting a user's password or MFA
playbooks.summary: Use when a caller posing as an employee convinced the service desk to reset a password or enroll a new MFA device, and the attacker may now hold that account.

preparation: Require identity verification by video with ID or a manager callback before MFA resets
Record help desk calls and log every reset with the ticket number
Alert the SOC on any MFA method change made by a help desk agent
identification: Pull the ticket and call recording for the reset and record the caller ID and verification answers
Confirm with the real employee through their manager that they did not call
Review sign-ins to the account after the reset for new IPs and devices
List actions taken by the account since the reset, such as mailbox, VPN or SaaS access
Search help desk tickets for other resets from the same caller number or pattern
containment: Disable the account and revoke all sessions
Remove the MFA device the attacker enrolled
Freeze further help desk resets for privileged accounts pending review
eradication: Reverse any access, group or role changes made by the attacker
Check whether the attacker used the account to call the help desk again for other users
Reset the account again with in-person verification for the real employee
recovery: Re-enable the employee with a phishing-resistant MFA method
Brief all help desk agents on the caller's script and number
Restore normal reset handling once new verification steps are in place
lessons: Record which verification step was weak or skipped and replace it
Add a detection for an MFA reset followed by sign-in from a new country within an hour
Measure how many resets are verified by video or manager callback

splunk.title: MFA method changes by help desk agents
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:aad:audit activityDisplayName IN ("Admin registered security info", "Admin deleted security info", "Reset user password", "Reset password (by admin)") earliest=-7d | table _time initiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName activityDisplayName targetResources{}.userPrincipalName

splunk.title: Sign-ins after the reset
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:aad:signin userPrincipalName=<suspect_user> earliest=<reset_time> | stats count values(appDisplayName) as apps by ipAddress location.countryOrRegion deviceDetail.displayName

playbooks.name: Employee access badge lost or stolen and possibly used
playbooks.summary: Use when a badge is reported lost or stolen, especially if badge logs show it being used after the report or in places the owner was not.

preparation: Give staff a 24-hour way to report a lost badge that reaches security immediately
Make sure badge deactivation takes effect on every reader within minutes
Check whether badges double as smart cards for workstation login
identification: Record when and where the badge was lost and when it was last used by the owner
Pull badge reader logs for the badge from the last known good use until now
Pull CCTV for any reader where the badge was used after it was reported lost
Check whether the badge holds a smart card certificate for logon or VPN
containment: Deactivate the badge in the access control system
Revoke any smart card certificate tied to the badge
Alert guards to stop anyone presenting that badge
eradication: Inspect areas entered with the badge after the loss for tampering or missing items
Check for logins to workstations near those doors at the matching times
Report the theft to police if the badge was stolen
recovery: Issue a new badge with a new card number to the employee
Confirm the old badge number shows as denied on readers
Review the employee's access level while issuing the new badge
lessons: Record the time between the loss and deactivation
Add an alert for any attempt to use a deactivated badge
Decide whether badges should show less information, such as the company name

splunk.title: Use of the badge since the last good use
splunk.spl: index=physical sourcetype=<badge_system> badge_id=<badge_id> earliest=<last_known_good> | table _time door event_type result

splunk.title: Attempts to use deactivated badges
splunk.spl: index=physical sourcetype=<badge_system> result=denied reason IN (inactive, lost, revoked) earliest=-30d | stats count values(door) as doors by badge_id cardholder

playbooks.name: Vishing calls to employees fishing for credentials or internal details
playbooks.summary: Use when several staff report phone calls from someone claiming to be IT, a vendor or an executive, asking for passwords, MFA codes, VPN details or internal information.

preparation: Publish a clear rule that IT never asks for passwords or MFA codes by phone
Keep phone system call detail records long enough to trace inbound calls
Give staff a quick reporting channel for suspicious calls
identification: Collect caller ID, time, pretext and questions asked from each reporting employee
Search call detail records for the same caller ID calling other extensions
Check whether any employee gave a password, MFA code or remote session
Note what internal details the caller already knew, such as names and system names
containment: Reset credentials for any employee who shared a password or code
Block the caller ID numbers on the phone system
Warn staff about the active campaign with the pretext used
eradication: Review sign-ins for employees who shared details for attacker activity
Report the numbers to the phone carrier
Restrict the internal directory information that the caller seemed to know
recovery: Confirm accounts of affected employees show only their own activity
Thank staff who reported and share how the pretext worked
Keep monitoring call detail records for the same numbers for 30 days
lessons: Record how the caller got staff direct dial numbers
Add a detection for one external number calling many internal extensions in a short period
Include the pretext in the next awareness session

splunk.title: External numbers calling many extensions
splunk.spl: index=voice sourcetype=<cdr_sourcetype> direction=inbound earliest=-7d | stats dc(called_extension) as extensions count by calling_number | where extensions>5 | sort - extensions

splunk.title: Sign-ins for employees who shared details
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:aad:signin userPrincipalName IN (<affected_users>) earliest=-3d | stats count values(ipAddress) as ips by userPrincipalName appDisplayName status.errorCode

playbooks.name: Sensitive documents recovered from trash or stolen from the office
playbooks.summary: Use when confidential paper records were found in open recycling or dumpsters, or someone was seen taking printouts, and you must work out what data was exposed.

preparation: Provide locked shred bins near printers and in every department
Use a certified shredding vendor with certificates of destruction
Enable secure print release so documents only print at the device when the user badges
identification: Inventory the recovered documents and classify the data types they contain
Identify the department and print job owners using print server logs
Determine how long the documents were exposed and who had access to the bin
Review CCTV of the bin area or dumpster for people searching it
containment: Secure the remaining documents and move the bin to a locked area
Collect any other unsecured documents in the same area
Notify the shredding vendor if their pickup was missed or bins were left open
eradication: Rotate any passwords, account numbers or access codes printed in the documents
Escalate to legal and privacy for a breach assessment if personal data was exposed
Report trespassing on the property to building management
recovery: Shred the recovered documents once the investigation no longer needs them
Confirm the department is using locked shred bins
Notify affected individuals if legal determines notice is required
lessons: Record which policy or vendor process failed
Add print server reports for large print jobs containing sensitive labels
Run a clean-desk and bin audit across offices

splunk.title: Print jobs matching the recovered documents
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Operational" EventCode=307 Document="*<document_name>*" | table _time host Param3 Param5 Param6

splunk.title: Large sensitive print jobs by user
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Operational" EventCode=307 earliest=-30d | stats count sum(Param8) as pages by Param3 | sort - pages

playbooks.name: Fake vendor technician gained access to the site
playbooks.summary: Use when someone posing as an HVAC, copier, elevator, ISP or IT vendor technician was let in, possibly into network closets, and their visit cannot be matched to any real work order.

preparation: Require vendors to be on a scheduled work order list held by reception and facilities
Escort all vendor technicians in network closets and data rooms
Keep a vendor contact list so reception can confirm a visit by phone
identification: Check the visitor log and the vendor's real dispatch team for the claimed work order
Pull CCTV and badge logs for the areas the technician entered
List all equipment the technician touched, opened or connected to
Interview staff who let the technician in and record what ID was shown
containment: Inspect every network closet, printer and device the technician accessed for added hardware
Shut network ports that show new devices since the visit
Alert reception at other sites to refuse entry to the same person
eradication: Remove and preserve any implanted device or altered cabling
Check copiers or printers serviced by the technician for firmware or address book changes
Report the impersonation to the real vendor and to police
recovery: Restore equipment configuration from backups if it was changed
Brief reception and facilities on the vendor verification steps
Confirm the network shows no new unknown devices for 14 days
lessons: Record which check would have stopped the entry and make it mandatory
Add an alert for network closet doors opened by visitor badges
Run a pretext test with a fake technician to measure reception's response

splunk.title: Door activity in network closets during the visit
splunk.spl: index=physical sourcetype=<badge_system> door IN (<closet_doors>) earliest=<visit_start> latest=<visit_end> | table _time door badge_id cardholder event_type

splunk.title: New MAC addresses on switches since the visit
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=DhcpSrvLog earliest=<visit_start> | stats min(_time) as first values(dest_ip) as ips by dest_mac | where first>=strptime("<visit_start>", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M") | convert ctime(first)

playbooks.name: USB drives found in the parking lot or lobby
playbooks.summary: Use when one or more unknown USB drives are found on the premises, possibly dropped deliberately, and someone may already have plugged one into a work computer.

preparation: Block mass storage USB devices on endpoints except approved encrypted models
Log USB device insertions with vendor and serial in EDR
Give staff a drop-off point for found media instead of plugging it in
identification: Collect all found drives, record where and when each was found, and bag them
Search EDR for any USB insertions of the same vendor and product IDs on endpoints
Analyze one drive on an isolated forensic workstation to see if it is storage or a keystroke injector
Check CCTV of the parking lot or lobby for who dropped the drives
containment: Isolate any endpoint where one of the drives was inserted
Block the drive's vendor and serial IDs in device control policy
Ask all staff to hand in any other found drives
eradication: Remove payloads or persistence from any endpoint where the drive ran
Reset credentials for users of affected endpoints
Preserve drives as evidence for law enforcement if malware is found
recovery: Return cleaned endpoints after EDR scans
Confirm device control policy applies to all endpoints
Tell staff the result and thank those who handed in drives
lessons: Record whether any drive was plugged in and why device control did not block it
Add a detection for HID devices that type commands immediately after insertion
Run a sanctioned USB drop test to measure staff behavior

splunk.title: USB insertions matching the found drives
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-PnP/Configuration" OR sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security EventCode IN (6416, 400) earliest=-7d | search DeviceDescription="*USB*" OR ClassName=DiskDrive | stats count values(host) as hosts by DeviceId DeviceDescription

splunk.title: Processes launched from removable drives
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_path IN ("D:\\*", "E:\\*", "F:\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path

playbooks.name: Caller posing as internal IT got an employee to install remote support
playbooks.summary: Use when someone phoned an employee claiming to be the company's IT department, often after spam floods, and walked them through opening Quick Assist or installing a remote tool.

preparation: Restrict Quick Assist and remote support tools to IT staff with application control
Tell staff how real IT contacts them and that IT always uses ticket numbers
Alert on new remote support sessions to workstations outside IT tickets
identification: Record the caller ID, the name the caller used and any ticket number they gave
Check whether the user received a spam flood or Teams message before the call
Find the remote session in EDR or the tool's logs and note start time and duration
List commands, scripts or files run during the session
Check whether the caller asked the user to sign in or approve MFA during the session
containment: Isolate the workstation and end the remote session
Revoke the user's sessions and reset their password
Block the remote tool's relay domains for unapproved use
eradication: Remove any tool, script or scheduled task left by the caller
Reimage the workstation if the caller ran unknown binaries
Check for lateral movement from the workstation using the user's credentials
recovery: Return the user to work on a clean device
Send staff a warning that describes the caller's script
Watch for repeat calls to the same department
lessons: Record whether Quick Assist was allowed for normal users and remove it if not needed
Add a detection for remote support sessions started shortly after an email bombing event
Decide whether IT should use an in-app verification step when calling users

splunk.title: Quick Assist and remote tools started by non-IT users
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as first from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN (quickassist.exe, anydesk.exe, screenconnect*.exe, teamviewer.exe) NOT Processes.user IN (<it_staff>) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | convert ctime(first)

splunk.title: Spam flood to the user before the call
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.recipient="<suspect_user>" by _time span=10m | where count>50

playbooks.name: After-hours unauthorized entry into the server room or data closet
playbooks.summary: Use when badge logs, alarms or CCTV show someone entering a server room, data center cage or wiring closet outside working hours without a change ticket.

preparation: Restrict server room badge access to a named list reviewed every quarter
Send server room door events and rack door sensors to the SIEM
Keep console and KVM login logs for servers in the room
identification: Identify the badge used and the holder's name and role
Pull CCTV for the room and note which racks the person opened
Check for an approved change ticket or on-call callout covering the entry
Review console, iLO, iDRAC and KVM logins during the entry window
Check switch logs for port changes and new links in the room at that time
containment: Suspend the badge pending review if the entry is unexplained
Inspect the opened racks for added devices, removed drives or cabling changes
Disable accounts used for console logins during the window
eradication: Remove and preserve any device added to the racks
Check servers for boot changes, new local accounts or USB insertions
Escalate to HR and legal if an employee entered without authorization
recovery: Restore server room access only to staff with a current need
Confirm all drives and hardware match the asset inventory
Re-enable accounts after password resets
lessons: Record why the badge had server room access and whether it should have
Add an alert for server room entry outside business hours without a linked change ticket
Review whether two-person rules are needed for the room

splunk.title: Server room entries outside business hours
splunk.spl: index=physical sourcetype=<badge_system> door IN (<server_room_doors>) result=granted earliest=-30d | eval hour=tonumber(strftime(_time, "%H")) | where hour<7 OR hour>19 | table _time door badge_id cardholder

splunk.title: Console and BMC logins during the entry
splunk.spl: index=* (sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=2) OR sourcetype=<bmc_audit> earliest=<entry_start> latest=<entry_end> | table _time host user Logon_Type src
